newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Spain's U.N. ambassador getting feet wet in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Spain's U.N. ambassador getting feet wet in Bosnia.

text.p: Carlos Westendorp, named on Friday as new high representative in Bosnia, said the key players in the Balkans would have to be persuaded to give up war criminals rather than have outside troops do it for them.

Westendorp, 60, Spain's ambassador to the United Nations and a former foreign minister, was chosen by states involved in the Bosnian peace process at a meeting in Sintra, Portugal, to replace Carl Bildt, 48, a former Swedish prime minister.

Asked about Bildt's stern warnings that war could erupt again unless indicted war criminals were brought to justice, Westendorp said, "This is quite right. You cannot start a real co-existence if this issue is still open."
But he said a "sheriff's action" by NATO-led peacekeeping troops was not the answer, saying he preferred "internal antibodies against an illness rather than outside bodies."
Westendorp, in a telephone interview, however, said he had no blueprint for the civilian operations in Bosnia and needed to get his feet wet first before he took over on June 20.
He said he thought long before accepting the post but was persuaded by friends and "many countries" to accept it, adding: "I cannot shy away from this because it is really a challenge."

With 30,000 NATO-led troops in Bosnia due to leave next June, the United States and its allies are increasingly concerned that their time for ensuring that fighting does not re-ignite next year is running out.
"The biggest problem i think is there are some people in the Balkans and in Bosnia who do not want to live together and our main task is to be to convince them," he said.

He said he had no position yet on whether NATO troops should stay on longer, saying efforts should be concentrated first "to take advantage of the 13 months ahead of us in order to create the conditions for their departure."
"More important than dates are benchmarks which need to be fulfilled," he added.
Westendorp, a native of Madrid, has a law degree and joined Spain's foreign service in 1964, working mainly in European affairs in Madrid and in Brussels.
He served as foreign minister for about six months, from December 1995 to May 1996 and was named Spain's chief U.N. representative a year ago.
